Text 1
Many teachers assign homework every evening, believing that regular practice at home is the surest way for students to master new material. A daily assignment, they argue, builds discipline and helps students notice what they have not yet understood before the next lesson. Without it, they warn, lessons fade quickly from memory and students fall behind.

Text 2
A review of studies on homework found little link between the amount of homework assigned in primary schools and pupils' test results. For older students the link was stronger, but only up to about two hours a night; beyond that, results did not improve. The researchers suggest that for young children, time spent reading for pleasure or playing outdoors may be just as valuable as written assignments.

Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the teachers' view in Text 1?
options: They would claim that older students should be given more than two hours of homework a night.
They would agree that students of every age benefit from homework that is assigned each evening.
They would say daily homework may help older students but does little for young children.
They would argue that homework lowers the test results of students in every age group.
explanation: The review found a link only for older students, and none beyond two hours, while young children gained little. It finds no benefit past two hours, not harm, so it neither supports homework for all ages nor claims homework lowers results.

Text 1
When astronomers voted in 2006 to reclassify Pluto as a "dwarf planet," many people protested. For them, Pluto had been the ninth planet since its discovery in 1930, and removing it seemed an arbitrary decision by a small committee. Some argued that tradition and public affection should count for something in deciding what a planet is.

Text 2
The reclassification of Pluto followed a simple scientific logic. Astronomers had discovered several objects in the outer solar system similar in size to Pluto, including one, Eris, that is slightly more massive. Either all of them had to be called planets, or a clear definition was needed. A planet, the astronomers decided, must have cleared its orbit of other large bodies, which Pluto has not done.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the protesters described in Text 1?
options: By arguing that Eris should also have been removed from the official list of planets
By agreeing that public affection should help decide which objects are called planets
By pointing out that Pluto is larger than every other object in the outer solar system
By explaining that the decision followed a consistent rule, not an arbitrary one
explanation: Text 2 presents the change as the result of a clear rule needed once similar objects were found, answering the charge of arbitrariness. It says Eris is more massive than Pluto, and it gives no weight to tradition or affection.

stem:
Text 1
Studies comparing reading on paper with reading on screens have often found that people remember less of what they read on a screen, especially long, complex texts. One explanation is that screens encourage skimming: readers used to scrolling quickly through messages bring the same hurried habits to serious reading, even when a text demands close attention.

Text 2
The so-called screen penalty may not be fixed. In a recent study, students who were told to read carefully and were given more time performed just as well on screens as on paper. The difference, the researchers concluded, lies less in the screen itself than in the reading habits people bring to it, and habits can be changed.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
options: It accepts the habit-based explanation in Text 1 but suggests that the effect can be overcome.
It argues that reading on paper encourages skimming even more than reading on screens does.
It offers new evidence that screens themselves damage readers' memory for complex texts.
It rejects the finding in Text 1 that people tend to remember less of what they read on screens.
explanation: Text 2 agrees that habits, not screens, cause the gap, and adds that changed instructions removed it. It does not deny the usual finding; it calls the penalty 'not fixed', which assumes the penalty normally exists.

Text 1
Modern zoos argue that they play an important role in conservation. By breeding endangered species in captivity, they keep alive populations that might otherwise disappear, and some animals bred in zoos, such as the Arabian oryx, have been successfully returned to the wild. Zoos also teach millions of visitors each year about the threats facing wildlife.

Text 2
Critics of zoos accept that a few breeding programmes have saved species from extinction. But they point out that most animals in zoos are not endangered at all, and only a small number of species have ever been released back into the wild. For the majority of animals kept in zoos, they argue, conservation is a justification rather than the true purpose.

Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 about conservation?
options: By arguing that no species has ever been saved from extinction by a zoo's breeding programme
By granting some successes while denying that conservation explains most of what zoos do
By agreeing that conservation is the main reason that most animals are kept in zoos today
By claiming that teaching visitors about wildlife matters more than breeding endangered species
explanation: The critics 'accept that a few breeding programmes have saved species' but say most zoo animals are not endangered, so conservation is mostly a justification. Saying no species was ever saved contradicts that concession.

Text 1
Several schools in Islamabad have proposed starting classes an hour later, at nine o'clock. Studies show that teenagers' body clocks shift during adolescence, making it hard for them to fall asleep early. Supporters believe that a later start would leave students more alert in lessons and, over time, improve their marks.

Text 2
Parents' groups have opposed the plan to start school later. Many parents leave for work at eight, and a later start would leave younger children unsupervised in the morning or force families to arrange extra transport. Whatever the benefits for sleep, they argue, a school timetable must also work for the families who depend on it.

Which choice best describes a difference in focus between the two texts?
options: Text 1 focuses on younger children, while Text 2 focuses on adults who work during the night.
Text 1 focuses on students' sleep, while Text 2 focuses on the practical needs of families.
Text 1 focuses on teachers' working hours, while Text 2 focuses on teenagers' changing body clocks.
Text 1 focuses on transport costs, while Text 2 focuses on the marks students get in examinations.
explanation: Text 1 supports the later start because of teenagers' body clocks and alertness, while Text 2 raises work schedules, supervision and transport. Transport appears only in Text 2, and body clocks only in Text 1.

Text 1
The symbols found on Indus Valley seals have resisted every attempt at decipherment. Most scholars assume that they record a written language, perhaps an early form of a language family still spoken in South Asia. The main obstacle is the shortness of the inscriptions: most contain only about five signs, and no text giving the same words in a known language has been found.

Text 2
A few researchers have questioned whether the Indus signs are writing at all. They note that the inscriptions are extremely short and that many signs appear only once in the entire known collection. Such signs, they suggest, might be symbols of clans, offices or gods, closer to emblems than to words.

Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption described in Text 1?
options: They would doubt it, citing the same feature that Text 1 treats as an obstacle to decipherment.
They would reject it, arguing that a bilingual text has shown the signs to be emblems.
They would support it, but argue that the language belonged to a different language family.
They would accept it, since very short inscriptions are typical of early written languages.
explanation: Text 1 sees short inscriptions as a barrier to reading the script, while Text 2 uses that same shortness to question whether it is writing at all. Text 1 says no bilingual text has been found, and Text 2 never claims one.

Text 1
Since 2020, many software companies in Lahore and Karachi have allowed their staff to work from home. Managers report that productivity has stayed the same or even risen, and employees save hours each week that they once spent commuting through heavy traffic. Several firms have given up part of their office space altogether.

Text 2
Working from home has costs that productivity figures do not show. Junior employees, in particular, say they learn less when they cannot watch experienced colleagues solve problems or ask quick questions at the next desk. Some companies have therefore begun asking new staff to spend at least three days a week in the office.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the managers' reports in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that working from home has no real disadvantages for any of the employees
By claiming that the time spent commuting in Lahore and Karachi has actually decreased
By suggesting that the reports may overlook a cost to less experienced workers
By arguing that productivity has in fact fallen sharply at most of these companies
explanation: Text 2 says productivity figures miss a hidden cost: junior staff learn less at home. It does not dispute the figures themselves, only what they leave out.

Text 1
At the end of the novel, Sameena leaves her village for the city, and most readers see the ending as a triumph. She has escaped the narrow expectations of her family and is free, at last, to pursue her studies. Her final words, a cheerful promise to write home every week, seem to confirm the note of hope.

Text 2
The ending is less triumphant than it first appears. In the final chapter, Sameena looks back at the village from the bus window and feels "something tear." The novelist gives her freedom, but she also makes clear what that freedom costs: the only home Sameena has ever known. Even the cheerful promise to write home reads, on a second look, like an attempt to hold on.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the ending in Text 1?
options: By claiming that Sameena's family supported her decision to move to the city
By arguing that Sameena does not actually leave her village at the end of the novel
By agreeing that the ending is a simple triumph with no sense of sadness in it
By accepting that Sameena gains freedom but stressing what she loses
explanation: Text 2 says 'The novelist gives her freedom' but points to the tearing feeling as a sign of what she loses. It calls the ending 'less triumphant', not untriumphant, so it qualifies rather than reverses Text 1's reading.

Text 1
Raising the minimum wage, some economists warn, can backfire. If employers must pay more for each worker, they may hire fewer people, cut working hours or replace workers with machines. The very workers the policy aims to help could then find themselves without jobs, or with less income than before the rise.

Text 2
Studies of actual minimum wage increases have often found much smaller job losses than simple models predict, and sometimes none at all. One reason may be that better-paid workers are less likely to quit, which saves employers the cost of constantly hiring and training replacements. Higher pay may also increase spending in local shops, creating demand that supports jobs.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the warning in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that higher minimum wages usually lead employers to replace workers with machines
By claiming that employers would rather hire and train new workers than keep their old ones
By noting that evidence from real wage rises often shows less harm than the warning predicts
By arguing that minimum wage increases always create a large number of new jobs for workers
explanation: Text 2 reports 'much smaller job losses than simple models predict' and suggests lower staff turnover as a reason. It does not say rises always create jobs; at best it found no losses in some cases.

Text 1
For most of the twentieth century, dinosaurs were pictured as scaly, slow-moving reptiles, more like giant lizards than any living animal. Museum models and films showed them dragging heavy tails along the ground. Their extinction was often treated as proof that they were evolutionary failures, too slow and clumsy to survive.

Text 2
Fossils discovered since the 1990s, many of them in China, have transformed our picture of dinosaurs. Some show clear traces of feathers, and studies of bones suggest that many dinosaurs were active and grew quickly. Most palaeontologists now regard birds as the living descendants of one group of dinosaurs, so in a sense dinosaurs never fully disappeared.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
options: It explains why dinosaurs died out, a question that Text 1 leaves completely unanswered.
It argues that the films mentioned in Text 1 were more accurate than the museum models.
It offers new fossil evidence that supports the picture of dinosaurs described in Text 1.
It presents discoveries that have replaced the older picture of dinosaurs given in Text 1.
explanation: Text 1 describes the old image of slow, scaly reptiles, and Text 2 reports feathered, active dinosaurs that 'transformed our picture'. The new fossils contradict rather than support the older image, and Text 2 does not discuss extinction.

Text 1
When a famous painting is cleaned, layers of yellowed varnish and old repairs are removed, and colours that viewers have not seen for centuries reappear. Restorers argue that this brings us closer to what the artist actually intended. To them, a cleaned painting is a rediscovered painting, finally free of the dirt of history.

Text 2
Cleaning a painting is never neutral. Some varnishes and glazes removed as "later additions" may have been applied by the artists themselves to soften their colours, and once removed, they cannot be put back. Critics of aggressive restoration argue that the brighter colours revealed may be further from the artist's intention, not closer.

Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the restorers' argument in Text 1?
options: By warning that cleaning may strip away the artist's own layers and distort the original
By arguing that paintings should be varnished again every few years to protect them
By claiming that most viewers prefer the yellowed colours of paintings left uncleaned
By agreeing that removing old varnish always reveals the colours the artist intended
explanation: The critics say some removed glazes may be the artist's own, so the cleaned result may be 'further from the artist's intention'. They say nothing about repeated varnishing or viewers' tastes.

stem:
Text 1
Historians once explained major events chiefly through the decisions of powerful individuals: kings, generals, revolutionary leaders. In this view, had a single leader chosen differently, the course of history might have changed entirely. Biographies of such figures filled library shelves for generations, while the lives of ordinary people received little attention.

Text 2
No leader acts alone. A general's victory depends on the harvests that feed his army, the roads that carry his supplies and the willingness of thousands of soldiers to follow orders. Yet it would be equally mistaken to treat leaders as mere puppets of such forces; at moments of crisis, one person's choice can tip a balance that conditions have already made fragile.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?
options: By arguing that ordinary soldiers, rather than leaders, made all of the important decisions
By granting that individuals matter while insisting their choices depend on conditions
By accepting it fully and adding that harvests and roads are of little importance to victory
By rejecting it completely and arguing that individual decisions never change the course of history
explanation: Text 2 stresses harvests, roads and soldiers, but says treating leaders as 'mere puppets' would be 'equally mistaken', since a choice can tip a fragile balance. That middle position rules out both total rejection and full acceptance.

Text 1
When the city banned thin plastic shopping bags, officials predicted a quick drop in the litter that blocks drains during the monsoon. Shoppers, they said, would soon get used to carrying cloth bags. The ban, they argued, was a simple and cheap way to protect the city's streets and waterways.

Text 2
A year after the ban on plastic bags, a survey of markets found that many shopkeepers were still handing them out. Inspections were rare, fines were small, and cloth bags cost more than many customers wanted to pay. The researchers concluded that a ban without proper enforcement changes very little.

Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the officials' prediction in Text 1?
options: By arguing that plastic bags do not in fact block the city's drains in the monsoon
By claiming that the fines for using plastic bags were too high to be fair
By agreeing that shoppers quickly switched to carrying cloth bags after the ban
By reporting that the weakly enforced ban had less effect than predicted
explanation: The survey found plastic bags still in use, with rare inspections and small fines, so the predicted quick change did not happen. Text 2 calls the fines small, not too high, and does not dispute that bags block drains.

stem:
Text 1
It is widely believed that children learn languages more easily than adults. Young children who move to a new country often speak the local language without an accent within a few years, while their parents may struggle for decades. For this reason, many schools introduce foreign languages as early as possible.

Text 2
In controlled studies, adults often learn the grammar and vocabulary of a new language faster than children, at least at first. Children's advantage appears mainly in pronunciation and in the level they eventually reach after many years of immersion. Whether children learn "more easily," then, depends on what is being measured and over what period.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief described in Text 1?
options: By suggesting that the belief holds for some aspects of learning but not others
By arguing that adults always reach a higher final level in a language than children
By claiming that pronunciation is the only part of a language that really matters
By agreeing that children learn every part of a new language faster than adults do
explanation: Text 2 gives adults the early lead in grammar and vocabulary but children the edge in pronunciation and final level, so the belief is only partly true. It credits children, not adults, with the higher eventual level.

stem:
Text 1
When a computer defeated the world chess champion in 1997, many commentators predicted that people would lose interest in the game. If machines could play better than any human, they asked, why would anyone want to watch humans play? Some even suggested that chess would become a historical curiosity, like a puzzle that had already been solved.

Text 2
Chess is more popular today than at any point in its history, with millions of people playing online every day. Computers have become training partners rather than rivals: young players study engine analysis to learn ideas that once took decades to discover, and viewers of top games follow an engine's evaluation bar to understand who is winning.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the commentators' prediction in Text 1?
options: By claiming that the computer had not really beaten the world champion in 1997
By noting that it has not come true and that computers have helped the game
By arguing that humans can still defeat the strongest chess computers in matches
By agreeing that machines have made human chess much less interesting to watch
explanation: Text 2 reports record popularity and describes computers as training and viewing aids, the opposite of the predicted decline. It never disputes the 1997 result or claims humans can beat engines.

Text 1
Sending humans to live on Mars, its supporters argue, would protect our species from disasters on Earth, such as an asteroid strike or a global pandemic. A self-sufficient colony would be a backup copy of human civilisation. The cost, though enormous, is small compared with what would be lost if humanity disappeared.

Text 2
Any disaster severe enough to make Earth uninhabitable would still leave it far more habitable than Mars, which has thin air, deadly radiation and no liquid water at its surface. Building shelters on Earth that could survive such events would be cheaper and easier than building a city on another planet. Exploring Mars may be worthwhile for science, but not as an insurance policy.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' argument in Text 1?
options: By claiming that a global pandemic could never make the Earth hard to live on
By arguing that humans should never explore Mars because the planet is so dangerous
By arguing that the same protection could be achieved more easily on Earth
By agreeing that a colony on Mars is the best protection against an asteroid strike
explanation: Text 2 argues that even a damaged Earth beats Mars and that shelters on Earth would be cheaper, so the backup goal is better met at home. It still calls exploring Mars 'worthwhile for science', which rules out the claim that humans should never go.

Text 1
For a long time, archaeologists believed that farming began in a single region, the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East, and spread outward from there to the rest of the world. Farming, in this view, was one great invention that other peoples copied as they learned of it from their neighbours.

Text 2
Evidence gathered over recent decades shows that farming arose independently in several places, including China, Mesoamerica and the highlands of New Guinea, each with its own crops, from rice and maize to taro. Rather than a single invention, agriculture appears to have been discovered again and again by different peoples.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
options: It agrees with Text 1 but adds that the Fertile Crescent was where rice and maize were first grown.
It challenges the view in Text 1 by presenting evidence of several separate origins.
It supports the view in Text 1 by showing how farming spread outward from one region.
It explains why farming failed to reach China, Mesoamerica and the highlands of New Guinea.
explanation: Text 1 describes one origin copied elsewhere, while Text 2 reports independent origins with different crops. The crops named belong to those other regions, and farming did develop there.

stem:
Text 1
Lahore is growing rapidly, and planners face a choice. Some argue that the city should build upward, allowing tall apartment towers near the centre. Taller buildings, they say, would house more people on less land, protecting farmland at the city's edges and shortening the journeys people make to work each day.

Text 2
Height alone does not make a city dense or efficient. Towers surrounded by car parks and wide roads can house fewer people per hectare than neighbourhoods of four- or five-storey buildings packed along narrow streets, like those of the old walled city. What matters most is how buildings are arranged, not simply how tall they are.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?
options: By arguing that Lahore should stop growing and protect its farmland with strict laws
By claiming that far too many people already live inside the old walled city
By agreeing that only tall towers can protect the farmland at the edges of the city
By questioning whether tall buildings are the best way to reach the density Text 1 wants
explanation: Text 2 shares the goal of housing many people on little land but argues that layout, not height, achieves it. The walled city is offered as a model of density, not a problem.

stem:
Text 1
To understand a poem, a reader must know what its author meant. Letters, diaries and interviews can reveal a poet's intentions, and a reading that contradicts them is simply a misreading. Without such evidence, interpretation becomes guesswork, with each reader inventing whatever meaning happens to suit them. Only the author, after all, knows what the poem was meant to say.

Text 2
Poets are not always the best guides to their own work. Many have admitted that they discovered what a poem meant only after writing it, and some changed their explanations over the years. The words on the page, which every reader can examine, are a firmer basis for interpretation than a poet's private statements, though those statements can still offer useful clues.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that a reading contradicting a poet's intentions is "simply a misreading"?
options: By arguing that the words on the page outweigh the poet's statements
By claiming that every reader's interpretation of a poem is equally valid
By arguing that readers should ignore a poet's letters and interviews completely
By agreeing that letters and diaries are the most reliable guides to what a poem means
explanation: Text 2 makes 'the words on the page' the firmer basis while granting that poets' statements 'can still offer useful clues'. That concession rules out ignoring them entirely, and preferring the text is not the same as accepting every reading.

Text 1
Pakistan's tree-planting campaigns have put hundreds of millions of saplings in the ground since 2014. Supporters say the programme will cool cities, reduce flooding and absorb carbon dioxide, and they point to the sheer number of trees planted as proof of its success. Officials publish planting totals each year, and every new record is announced as a victory for the environment.

Text 2
Counting saplings says little about a forest. Many young trees die within a year if they are not watered or protected from grazing animals, and trees planted in the wrong places, such as natural grasslands, can harm the ecosystems already there. A better measure of success is how many trees survive, and where they grow.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' evidence in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that planting large numbers of trees always cools cities and reduces floods
By claiming that young trees rarely die once they have been planted in the ground
By arguing that the number of saplings planted is a poor measure of success
By arguing that Pakistan should stop planting trees and protect its grasslands instead
explanation: Text 2 says counting saplings 'says little' and proposes survival and location as better measures. It warns against planting on grasslands, not against planting altogether, and it says many saplings die.

stem:
Text 1
Students who take notes on laptops can type nearly everything a lecturer says, and many assume this makes their notes more useful. A widely cited study, however, found that students who took notes by hand did better on questions requiring understanding. Writing by hand is slower, the researchers argued, which forces students to summarise ideas in their own words.

Text 2
Attempts to repeat the famous note-taking study have produced mixed results. Several found little or no difference between handwritten and typed notes once students had reviewed their notes before the test. What may matter most is not the tool but what students do with it: summarising and reviewing help, whatever the method.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the study described in Text 1?
options: By suggesting its result may not hold and that habits matter more than tools
By arguing that typed notes are always more useful because they are more complete
By agreeing that writing by hand always leads to better understanding than typing
By claiming that reviewing notes before a test makes little difference to results
explanation: Text 2 reports mixed replications and says reviewing and summarising matter more than the method. It credits reviewing with helping, so it does not dismiss it, and it favours neither tool.

Text 1
Many public libraries charge fines for overdue books. Librarians who support the fines argue that without them, borrowers would keep books for months, leaving other readers waiting. The small charge, they say, reminds people that a library book belongs to everyone, not just to the person who happens to have it.

Text 2
When a city library system abolished overdue fines, most borrowed books still came back on time, and thousands of former members who had stopped visiting because of unpaid fines returned. Fines, the library concluded, had mainly kept the poorest readers away rather than speeding up returns. Staff time once spent chasing small debts now goes to helping readers.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the librarians' argument in Text 1?
options: By claiming that most borrowers would rather buy books than borrow them
By agreeing that borrowers keep books for months whenever no fines are charged
By arguing that libraries should raise their fines to bring back former members
By reporting that removing fines did not cause the long delays they feared
explanation: In Text 2, books 'still came back on time' after fines ended, contradicting the predicted months-long delays. Members returned because fines were removed, so raising fines would have the opposite effect.

stem:
Text 1
Expertise, according to a popular idea, comes from practice: roughly ten thousand hours of it. On this view, talent matters little; almost anyone who practises long and hard enough can reach the top of a field such as music or chess. Stories of famous performers who practised from early childhood are often offered as proof.

Text 2
Practice is essential, but it is not the whole story. In studies of chess players and musicians, the amount of practice explains only part of the differences between performers; some reach expert level with far fewer hours than others. Factors such as the age at which training begins and inborn differences in memory also appear to matter.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the popular idea described in Text 1?
options: By arguing that practice makes no real difference to how skilled a performer becomes
By agreeing that practice matters while denying that it alone explains expertise
By claiming that inborn memory is the only thing that separates experts from others
By agreeing that anyone who practises ten thousand hours will become an expert
explanation: Text 2 calls practice 'essential' but 'not the whole story', adding age and inborn memory. Memory is one of several factors it mentions, not the only one.

Text 1
Popular films and older history books often show the pyramids of Egypt being built by armies of slaves driven by whips. The image fits a common picture of ancient kings as rulers who could force thousands of people to work for them without any reward or care. Few viewers ever question it.

Text 2
Excavations near the pyramids at Giza have uncovered the remains of workers' villages, with bakeries and cemeteries where labourers were buried with bread and beer for the afterlife. Some skeletons show injuries that had been treated and had healed. Most archaeologists now think the builders were organised, fed and cared for, perhaps as paid workers or as farmers serving in shifts.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
options: It supports the picture in Text 1 with evidence of how harshly the builders were treated.
It argues that the films mentioned in Text 1 are more accurate than older history books.
It presents evidence that challenges the picture of the builders given in Text 1.
It explains how the pyramids were designed, a subject that Text 1 does not discuss.
explanation: The villages, burials and healed injuries in Text 2 suggest cared-for workers, contradicting Text 1's whipped slaves. The healed injuries show medical care, not harsh treatment, and design is never discussed.

Text 1
Universities should rely less on entrance tests, some educators argue. A single exam, taken on one morning, can be affected by illness, nerves or the coaching that wealthier families can afford. School grades earned over several years, they say, give a fairer picture of a student's ability, since one bad day cannot outweigh years of steady work.

Text 2
School grades have their own problems. Standards differ widely between schools, and some schools award high marks far more generously than others. A common entrance test, whatever its flaws, measures every applicant against the same yardstick, which can help talented students from little-known schools stand out. Abolishing it could hurt the very applicants the educators hope to protect.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the educators' proposal in Text 1?
options: By arguing that grades are unreliable too and that a shared test offers one standard
By claiming that entrance tests are never affected by nerves, illness or private coaching
By arguing that universities should rely only on interviews with each applicant
By agreeing that school grades give the fairest possible picture of a student's ability
explanation: Text 2 points out that grading standards vary and that a common test uses 'the same yardstick'. It admits the test has flaws, so it does not claim tests are free of nerves or coaching effects.

stem:
Text 1
Experienced firefighters, nurses and pilots often make life-or-death decisions in seconds, without consciously weighing their options. Researchers who have studied them argue that such intuition is not mysterious: it is pattern recognition built from years of practice, and in familiar situations it can outperform slow, careful analysis. Training programmes, they suggest, should value such judgment.

Text 2
Intuition deserves trust only in certain conditions. It is reliable when people work in settings that are regular and give quick, clear feedback, as firefighting does. In fields where outcomes are unpredictable and feedback is slow, such as long-term stock-market forecasting, experts' confident hunches are often no better than chance.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the researchers' argument in Text 1?
options: By accepting it fully and adding that stock-market experts also have reliable hunches
By rejecting it and arguing that intuition is no better than chance in firefighting
By accepting it for settings like firefighting while denying it holds in every field
By arguing that slow analysis is always more reliable than intuition in any situation
explanation: Text 2 names firefighting as a setting where intuition is reliable but says hunches fail where feedback is slow, as in stock forecasting. It reserves 'no better than chance' for those unpredictable fields, not firefighting.

Text 1
Karachi's colonial-era stone buildings, with their carved balconies and arched windows, are disappearing as owners demolish them to build modern towers. Heritage campaigners argue that the city should make it illegal to demolish any building more than a hundred years old. Once such a building is gone, they point out, it can never be replaced.

Text 2
Owners of old buildings in Karachi often have good reasons to sell. Many of the buildings are crumbling, rents are kept at tiny amounts by old agreements, and repairs cost more than the buildings earn. Protecting heritage, these owners argue, will work only if the city also helps pay for upkeep; a ban alone simply leaves buildings to collapse.

Based on the texts, how would the owners in Text 2 most likely respond to the campaigners' proposal in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that banning demolition is the simplest way to protect the city's heritage
By arguing that old buildings have no historical value and should all be replaced
By claiming that the rents charged for old buildings in Karachi are far too high
By arguing that a ban without financial help would fail to save the buildings
explanation: The owners say 'a ban alone simply leaves buildings to collapse' and ask for help with upkeep. They accept the goal of protecting heritage, and they describe rents as tiny, not too high.

stem:
Text 1
Breakfast is often called the most important meal of the day. Many people believe that skipping it leads to weight gain, because those who miss breakfast become so hungry that they overeat later. Advertisements for cereals have repeated this message for decades, and many parents insist that children eat something before school.

Text 2
In a trial in which adults were randomly assigned to eat or skip breakfast for several months, the two groups lost or gained similar amounts of weight. The researchers concluded that, for weight at least, whether a person eats breakfast matters less than what and how much they eat across the whole day.

Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1 that skipping breakfast leads to weight gain?
options: By claiming that what people eat during the day has little effect on their weight
By noting that their trial found no clear weight difference between the groups
By arguing that eating breakfast makes people gain more weight than skipping it
By agreeing that people who skip breakfast tend to overeat later and gain weight
explanation: Both groups' weight changed similarly, so the trial gives no support for the belief. The researchers stress that daily food intake matters, the opposite of saying daily intake has little effect.

stem:
Text 1
Computer programs can now produce paintings in the style of famous artists within seconds. Some critics insist that such images cannot be art, because art requires a human being with something to express. A machine, they argue, has no experiences, no feelings and therefore nothing to say. However pleasing the result, it is decoration rather than art.

Text 2
Whether a machine "means" anything may matter less than it seems. People write the instructions, select among hundreds of results and decide which images to show. Photography faced a similar objection in the nineteenth century, when critics claimed that a camera merely copied the world; today few would deny that a great photograph can be art.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics' argument in Text 1?
options: By claiming that photography is still not accepted as a form of art by critics
By suggesting that the people guiding the program may supply the expression needed
By arguing that machines have experiences and feelings of their own to express
By agreeing that images made with a computer can never be considered works of art
explanation: Text 2 shifts attention to the human choices behind the images and compares the case to photography, which is now accepted as art. It does not claim machines have feelings; it says their lack may 'matter less than it seems'.

Text 1
Children should first learn to read in the language they speak at home, many educators argue. A child in rural Sindh who speaks Sindhi at home but is taught to read in English must learn a new language and a new skill at the same time, and many fall behind. Reading skills learned in a familiar language, they add, transfer readily to a second one.

Text 2
Parents in many parts of Pakistan want their children taught in English from the start, believing it offers the best chance of a good job. Their concern is understandable. Yet studies from several countries suggest that children taught first in their home language often end up reading English better than those taught in English from the beginning.

Based on the texts, how would the educators in Text 1 most likely respond to the parents described in Text 2?
options: By arguing that children in rural Sindh do not need to learn English at all
By claiming that Urdu is more useful than English for finding a good job
By arguing that starting with the home language may best serve their goal
By agreeing that children should be taught to read in English from their first day
explanation: The educators believe reading skills transfer to a second language, which fits Text 2's finding that home-language starters often read English better. So they would say the parents' aim, strong English, is best reached that way; they never reject English itself.

stem:
Text 1
Several countries have banned mobile phones in schools, and supporters report calmer classrooms, fewer distractions and less online bullying during the school day. Teachers say pupils talk to one another more at break time instead of staring at screens. In the supporters' view, the benefits are so obvious that no further evidence is needed.

Text 2
Studies of phone bans have found mixed effects on test scores: some schools improved, others saw no change. A ban may also remove a useful tool, since phones can be used for research or language apps when teachers plan for them. Clear rules about when phones may be used, rather than a total ban, may offer the benefits without the losses.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' view in Text 1?
options: By claiming that online bullying has increased in schools that have banned phones
By arguing that phones cause no distraction at all in modern school classrooms
By agreeing that phone bans have clearly raised pupils' test scores in every school
By suggesting that a total ban may not be needed to gain its benefits
explanation: Text 2 reports mixed results and proposes clear rules that 'may offer the benefits without the losses'. It says some schools saw no change in scores, so it does not claim bans raised scores everywhere.

stem:
Text 1
Wind turbines are often criticised for killing birds. Opponents of new wind farms along the coast of Sindh point to images of birds struck by spinning blades and argue that the turbines pose an unacceptable threat to wildlife, especially to the migrating species that pass through the region each winter.

Text 2
Turbines do kill birds, but the numbers need context. Studies in several countries have found that far more birds die from collisions with buildings, from cats and from power lines than from wind turbines. Careful siting, away from major migration routes, can reduce the risk further. Fossil-fuel power, meanwhile, harms birds through pollution and climate change.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the opponents' argument in Text 1?
options: By accepting that turbines kill birds while arguing that the threat is relatively small
By agreeing that wind turbines are the most serious danger facing migrating birds
By denying that wind turbines are responsible for the deaths of any birds at all
By arguing that new wind farms should be built directly on major migration routes
explanation: Text 2 begins 'Turbines do kill birds' but compares them with larger causes such as buildings and cats. It recommends siting turbines away from migration routes, not on them.

stem:
Text 1
Pakistani schools are often criticised for relying on rote learning. Students memorise answers word for word, critics say, and can repeat definitions without understanding them. Such a system, they argue, produces graduates who struggle with unfamiliar problems. Examinations that reward exact repetition only make the problem worse, since teachers naturally teach to the test.

Text 2
Memorisation has a poor reputation, but it is not the enemy of understanding. Fluent recall of basic facts, such as multiplication tables or key vocabulary, frees the mind to think about harder problems. The trouble arises when memorising becomes the only goal, and students are never asked to use what they have learned.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that rote learning alone is harmful while defending some memorisation
By agreeing that memorising multiplication tables stops students from understanding
By claiming that Pakistani examinations already reward understanding over recall
By arguing that students should never be asked to memorise facts or definitions
explanation: Text 2 defends recall of basic facts but locates 'the trouble' where memorising is the only goal, which matches part of the critics' concern. It praises learning tables, so it does not see them as a barrier to understanding.

stem:
Text 1
Bans on plastic straws have spread to cafés and cities around the world. Supporters say that straws, which are used for a few minutes and then thrown away, are an easy place to start cutting plastic waste, and that a visible ban encourages people to think about plastic in general.

Text 2
Plastic straws make up only a tiny fraction of the plastic that reaches the oceans; abandoned fishing nets and other gear make up a far larger share of the plastic floating at sea. Focusing on straws, critics worry, may let governments and companies appear active while the largest sources of ocean plastic go unaddressed.

Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' reasoning in Text 1?
options: By claiming that fishing gear makes up only a tiny share of the plastic in the oceans
By agreeing that straws are the main source of the plastic that reaches the oceans
By arguing that plastic straws should be encouraged because they are so convenient
By warning that a focus on straws may distract from much larger sources of pollution
explanation: The critics say straws are a 'tiny fraction' and fear the bans let larger sources such as fishing gear go unaddressed. They describe fishing gear, not straws, as the larger share.

stem:
Text 1
Historical novelists, some readers complain, take too many liberties. When a novel invents conversations between real Mughal emperors or changes the order of battles, readers who know little history may come away believing things that never happened. A novelist who writes about real people, these readers argue, owes them accuracy.

Text 2
A historical novel is not a history book, and readers generally know it. Its task is to imagine what the past felt like from inside: what a servant feared or a prince desired. Inventing dialogue is unavoidable, since no record preserves most conversations. Changing well-documented facts is another matter, however, and a good novelist explains such changes in an author's note.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the readers' complaint in Text 1?
options: By rejecting it entirely, since novelists may change any historical fact they like
By arguing that readers of historical novels usually believe everything they read
By defending invented dialogue while saying changed facts need explaining
By accepting it entirely, since novelists should never invent conversations for real people
explanation: Text 2 calls invented dialogue 'unavoidable' but treats changing documented facts as 'another matter' that needs an author's note. It thus splits the complaint, answering one part and partly accepting the other, and it says readers 'generally know' a novel is not history.

stem:
Text 1
Few people cycle to work in Lahore, and city officials say the reason is simple: residents prefer the comfort of cars and motorcycles. Building cycle lanes, they argue, would waste money on roads that almost no one would use. The heat of the summer months, they add, makes cycling unattractive for much of the year.

Text 2
In cities that have built safe, connected cycle lanes, the number of cyclists has often risen sharply within a few years. Surveys suggest that many people would cycle if they did not fear sharing roads with fast traffic. Low numbers of cyclists today may reflect dangerous roads more than people's preferences.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the officials' argument in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that the residents of Lahore will always prefer cars and motorcycles
By suggesting that few people cycle because the roads feel unsafe
By arguing that the summer heat in Lahore makes cycling dangerous to people's health
By claiming that cycle lanes are too expensive for most cities to build and maintain
explanation: Text 2 says low cycling 'may reflect dangerous roads more than people's preferences', directly challenging the officials' explanation. It does not discuss heat or cost.

stem:
Text 1
Woolly mammoths disappeared from most of their range around ten thousand years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age. Many scientists blame the changing climate: as the cold grasslands on which mammoths fed gave way to forests and wetlands, their food supply shrank and their populations collapsed, leaving only small groups on remote islands.

Text 2
Mammoths had survived earlier warm periods, which suggests that climate alone may not explain their disappearance. Their decline also coincided with the spread of human hunters across northern Europe, Asia and the Americas. Many researchers now think that a combination of shrinking habitat and hunting, rather than either factor alone, pushed mammoth populations past the point of recovery.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that climate change alone fully explains why the mammoths disappeared
By arguing that climate change was probably one cause among others
By rejecting the idea that the climate changed at the end of the last Ice Age
By claiming that human hunters were the only cause of the mammoths' extinction
explanation: Text 2 keeps shrinking habitat as a factor but adds hunting, 'rather than either factor alone'. That rules out both 'climate alone' and 'hunters were the only cause'.

Text 1
Tourism has brought new income to valleys such as Hunza and Swat. Families who once relied only on farming now run guest houses, restaurants and jeep services, and many young people no longer need to leave for the cities to find work. Local shops now stock goods that were hard to find a decade ago.

Text 2
The boom in tourism has had costs that visitors rarely see. In some valleys, hotels have been built on riverbanks prone to flooding, rubbish left by visitors piles up on mountain trails, and the price of land has risen beyond the reach of local families. Without planning, residents warn, tourism could damage the very landscapes that attract it.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
options: It explains why many young people from the valleys are still moving to the cities.
It rejects the claim in Text 1 that tourism has brought any new income to the valleys.
It provides further examples of the economic benefits that Text 1 has described.
It points to drawbacks of a development whose benefits Text 1 describes.
explanation: Text 1 lists tourism's economic gains, and Text 2 describes hidden costs such as flood-prone hotels, litter and land prices. Text 2 never denies the new income; it adds what that income has cost.

stem:
Text 1
Reading literary fiction, some psychologists claim, makes people more empathetic. In one study, participants who read a short literary story scored higher on a test of recognising others' emotions than participants who read non-fiction or nothing at all. Fiction, the researchers suggested, trains readers to imagine the minds of others.

Text 2
Later attempts to repeat that study often failed to find the same short-term effect. Yet surveys consistently show that people who read a great deal of fiction over their lives tend to score higher on measures of empathy. Whether reading causes empathy, or empathetic people simply enjoy fiction more, remains unclear.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
options: By arguing that readers of fiction are in fact less empathetic than other people
By agreeing that a single literary story reliably makes its readers more empathetic
By noting that a link exists but that its direction of cause is uncertain
By claiming that the surveys prove that reading fiction makes people more empathetic
explanation: Text 2 reports failed replications but a consistent link in surveys, then says it is unclear whether reading causes empathy or the reverse. The surveys show an association, which is exactly why Text 2 does not treat them as proof.

stem:
Text 1
Competitive video gaming, or e-sports, now fills stadiums and offers prize money in the millions. Its fans argue that it should be recognised as a sport: top players train for hours each day, work in teams and need lightning-fast reactions. Some international sporting events have even begun to include it.

Text 2
Whatever the skill involved, e-sports lack the physical exertion that most definitions of sport require. Chess also demands training and quick thinking, and is sometimes played in teams, yet few people call it a sport in the same sense as football or athletics. E-sports, on this view, are better described as competitive games.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the fans' argument in Text 1?
options: By arguing that skill and training are not enough without physical effort
By arguing that e-sports players need no real skill or training in order to succeed
By claiming that chess requires more physical exertion than football or athletics do
By agreeing that e-sports should count as sports because their players train so hard
explanation: Text 2 grants the skill ('Whatever the skill involved') but says sport requires physical exertion, using chess as a parallel. It never denies that players are skilled.

stem:
Text 1
School uniforms, their supporters argue, reduce competition over clothes. When every pupil wears the same shirt and trousers, children from poorer families are less likely to be teased, and parents are spared the cost of buying fashionable outfits. Uniforms also give pupils a sense of belonging to their school and to one another.

Text 2
Uniforms can be surprisingly expensive. Many schools require blazers, ties and badges bought only from a single approved shop, which often charges far more than ordinary clothing stores. For poorer families, these costs can outweigh any savings on everyday clothes, especially when growing children outgrow their uniforms every single year.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' claim in Text 1 about cost?
options: By pointing out that uniforms themselves can be costly for poorer families
By arguing that children from poorer families are teased more when wearing uniforms
By agreeing that uniforms always save families money on their children's clothing
By claiming that approved shops sell uniforms more cheaply than other clothing stores
explanation: Text 2 says approved-shop prices can 'outweigh any savings', answering the claim that uniforms spare parents expense. It says those shops charge more, not less, and it does not discuss teasing.

stem:
Text 1
Urban beekeeping has become popular in many cities, and supporters present it as a way to help pollinators. Rooftop hives, they say, give bees a refuge from the pesticides of the countryside and help reverse the decline of bee populations. Many companies now place hives on office roofs as a sign of their concern for nature.

Text 2
Honeybees are farmed animals, not endangered wildlife, and adding hives to a city can harm the wild bees that are actually in decline. Honeybees compete with wild species for the same flowers, and in some cities with many hives, researchers have found fewer wild bees. Planting more flowers would help pollinators more than adding hives.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' view in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that rooftop hives are the best way to reverse the decline of bees
By claiming that wild bees compete with honeybees for space on city rooftops
By arguing that adding hives may harm the wild bees most in need of help
By arguing that pesticides in the countryside pose no threat to bees of any kind
explanation: Text 2 says honeybees are not the declining species and compete with wild bees for flowers, so more hives can hurt the bees that need help. The competition is for flowers, not rooftop space, and pesticides are not discussed.

stem:
Text 1
Cheap, fashionable clothing has made it possible for more people than ever to dress well. Shoppers who once owned a few outfits can now buy new styles every season at low prices, and clothing factories have created millions of jobs in countries such as Bangladesh and Pakistan. For many young women there, a factory wage is their first independent income.

Text 2
The low price of fast fashion hides its real cost. Garments are often worn only a few times before being thrown away, and producing them uses large amounts of water and dye that can pollute rivers near factories. Many factory workers, too, earn low wages in difficult and sometimes dangerous conditions.

Which choice best describes a difference between the two texts?
options: Text 1 criticises shoppers, while Text 2 criticises the governments of factory countries.
Text 1 discusses clothing made in Bangladesh, while Text 2 discusses clothing made in Europe.
Text 1 stresses the pollution from factories, while Text 2 stresses the jobs they create.
Text 1 stresses the benefits of cheap clothing, while Text 2 stresses its hidden costs.
explanation: Text 1 praises low prices and new jobs; Text 2 turns to waste, pollution and low wages. The option giving Text 1 pollution and Text 2 jobs swaps the two texts' points.

stem:
Text 1
Every child should learn to write computer code, some educators say. Coding teaches logical thinking, and in a world run by software, students who cannot code will be at a disadvantage in the job market. Several countries have already made it a required school subject, often starting in the first years of primary school.

Text 2
Teaching coding to every pupil assumes that today's programming skills will still be needed when they start work. Yet tools that write code automatically are improving quickly. What may last longer is the ability to break problems into steps and check whether a solution works, skills that can be taught through mathematics and science as well as through coding.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the educators' proposal in Text 1?
options: By arguing that logical thinking is no longer a useful skill for most students
By suggesting the lasting value lies in problem-solving skills, not coding as such
By claiming that mathematics and science should be removed from school timetables
By agreeing that every child must learn to code in order to find a good job
explanation: Text 2 doubts that specific coding skills will last but values breaking problems into steps, which other subjects can teach too. It values logical thinking rather than dismissing it, and it names mathematics and science as ways to teach it.

stem:
Text 1
For a long time, archaeologists regarded art as a sign of the uniquely modern human mind. Neanderthals, in this view, were capable hunters but lacked the imagination needed to create symbols or decorate objects. The painted caves of France and Spain were credited entirely to our own species, Homo sapiens.

Text 2
Red pigment markings in caves in Spain have been dated to more than 64,000 years ago, before modern humans are thought to have reached the region. If the dates are correct, the markings were made by Neanderthals. Some researchers question the dating method, but if it holds, the line between Neanderthal and modern human minds may be less sharp than once believed.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?
options: By suggesting that new evidence may challenge it, if the dating holds
By stating that the view has been conclusively disproved by the discoveries in Spain
By arguing that modern humans made the Spanish markings before Neanderthals arrived
By agreeing that Neanderthals lacked the imagination needed to create any symbols
explanation: Text 2 says the markings would be Neanderthal 'if the dates are correct' and notes doubts about the method, so it challenges the view only conditionally. 'Conclusively disproved' ignores those repeated 'if' clauses.

stem:
Text 1
Bottled water is often marketed as purer and healthier than tap water. Many families in Pakistani cities buy it for drinking, believing that the water from their taps is unsafe. Sales of bottled water have risen steadily for years, and new brands appear on shop shelves almost every single month.

Text 2
In many cities, tap water is in fact contaminated, often because old pipes leak and allow sewage to seep in. Bottled water is a reasonable choice for families in such places. But some brands of bottled water have themselves failed quality tests, and boiling tap water is a cheaper way to make it safer to drink.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the families' belief in Text 1?
options: By claiming that every brand of bottled water has failed official quality tests
By arguing that tap water in Pakistani cities is always clean and safe to drink
By agreeing their tap water may be unsafe but noting bottled water can fail too
By arguing that boiling tap water makes it more dangerous than bottled water
explanation: Text 2 confirms that tap water is often contaminated but warns that 'some brands' of bottled water have failed tests. 'Some brands' is not every brand, and boiling is offered as a cheaper way to make water safer.

stem:
Text 1
Museums should charge no entry fee, many campaigners argue. Culture belongs to everyone, and even a small fee keeps away families with little money. When some national museums abroad stopped charging, visitor numbers rose sharply. A museum that charges for entry, the campaigners say, is a museum for the wealthy.

Text 2
Free entry does raise visitor numbers, but studies suggest that most of the extra visitors are people who already visited museums often, rather than new visitors from poorer backgrounds. Reaching those families may require other steps, such as school trips, events in local languages and exhibitions about their own communities.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the campaigners' argument in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that free entry alone will bring families with little money to museums
By granting that free entry raises numbers while doubting it reaches poorer families
By arguing that museums should raise their fees to pay for school trips and events
By denying that removing entry fees increases the number of people visiting museums
explanation: Text 2 accepts the rise in visitors but says most are existing museum-goers, so other steps are needed to reach poorer families. It does not deny the rise or suggest higher fees.

stem:
Text 1
Large dams on the Indus and its tributaries supply a significant share of Pakistan's electricity and store water for farming. Supporters of new dams argue that more storage is urgently needed, since the country can hold only a small fraction of its yearly river flow, and much of the monsoon water runs unused to the sea.

Text 2
Large dams bring benefits but also lasting problems. Their reservoirs gradually fill with silt, reducing storage, and the reduced flow of water and sediment downstream has contributed to the shrinking of the Indus delta, where seawater now pushes further inland. Any plan for new dams, critics say, must account for these costs.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
options: It rejects the claim in Text 1 that dams store water and produce electricity.
It provides more evidence that new dams are urgently needed across Pakistan.
It explains how the turbines inside a large dam produce electricity.
It raises costs that should be weighed against the benefits described in Text 1.
explanation: Text 2 opens by granting that dams 'bring benefits' and then adds silting and delta loss as costs to weigh. It accepts, rather than rejects, Text 1's points about storage and power.

stem:
Text 1
Some popular books describe forests as communities in which trees "talk" to one another, sharing food with their young and warning neighbours of danger through underground fungal networks. In this picture, a forest is less a collection of competitors than a cooperative family in which older trees care for younger ones.

Text 2
Fungal networks linking tree roots are real, and some chemicals do pass between trees through them. But recent reviews argue that the evidence for trees deliberately sharing food or sending warnings is weak, and that many field studies have been overstated in popular accounts. The fungi may simply be serving their own interests, trading nutrients for sugar.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the picture of forests in Text 1?
options: By denying that fungal networks connect the roots of different trees at all
By accepting that the networks exist while doubting that trees use them to cooperate
By arguing that trees compete with fungi for nutrients more than with each other
By agreeing that trees share food with their young through fungal networks
explanation: Text 2 says the networks 'are real' but calls the evidence for deliberate sharing and warning 'weak'. It suggests the fungi trade nutrients for their own benefit; it does not describe trees competing with fungi.

stem:
Text 1
Money, a famous study suggested, buys happiness only up to a point. Once people earned enough to cover their basic needs and some comforts, further increases in income made little difference to how happy they said they felt from day to day. The finding was widely reported as proof that chasing a higher salary is pointless.

Text 2
A more recent study, which asked people about their feelings many times a day, found that happiness kept rising with income well beyond the earlier limit, at least for most people. Only among the unhappiest group did the effect level off. The two studies may differ less than they seem: money appears to help most people, but it cannot cure every kind of unhappiness.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the finding described in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that income stops affecting happiness for everyone above a certain level
By claiming that the unhappiest people gain the most happiness from higher incomes
By suggesting that it holds mainly for an unhappy minority, not for most people
By arguing that money has no effect at all on how happy most people feel each day
explanation: Text 2 finds happiness rising with income for most people and levelling off 'only among the unhappiest group', which is where the earlier limit seems to apply. It says the effect levels off for the unhappiest, so they gain least, not most.

stem:
Text 1
Many young Pakistanis now write Urdu in the Roman alphabet when texting, and some commentators fear this will weaken the Urdu script. If people grow used to typing "kya haal hai" in Roman letters, they argue, fewer will bother to read and write in Nastaliq, and a rich written tradition will slowly fade.

Text 2
Roman Urdu on phones may reflect convenience rather than a rejection of the script. Early mobile keyboards did not support Urdu well, so people adapted. Now that Urdu keyboards are widely available, some surveys suggest that younger users switch between scripts depending on the situation, using Roman letters for quick messages and Urdu script for more formal writing.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the commentators' fear in Text 1?
options: By suggesting the habit is practical and need not mean the script is abandoned
By claiming that Urdu keyboards are still unavailable on most mobile phones
By agreeing that Roman Urdu will soon replace the Urdu script in formal writing
By arguing that young Pakistanis should stop sending text messages in Urdu
explanation: Text 2 explains Roman Urdu as a response to old keyboards and reports users keeping Urdu script for formal writing. It says Urdu keyboards are now 'widely available', the reverse of saying they are still unavailable.

stem:
Text 1
Several companies that tested a four-day working week reported that employees were less tired and more focused, and that the amount of work completed hardly fell. Managers at these firms say the shorter week has made it easier to keep good staff, and some have decided to keep it permanently.

Text 2
Results from four-day week trials should be read with care. Most companies that took part chose to do so, and many were office-based firms whose work could be reorganised easily. Hospitals, factories and shops, where someone must be present for every hour of opening, may find the change far harder to make.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the results reported in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that every business could easily move to a four-day working week
By arguing that the companies' employees were in fact more tired than before
By claiming that hospitals and factories already work only four days a week
By warning that the results may not apply to every kind of workplace
explanation: Text 2 notes that the firms chose to take part and were mostly offices, so the results may not carry over to hospitals or shops. It does not dispute the reported results themselves.

stem:
Text 1
Automation, some economists warn, will soon eliminate millions of jobs. Self-driving trucks, automated checkouts and software that writes reports could replace drivers, cashiers and clerks within a generation, leaving many workers with no obvious place in the economy. Unlike earlier machines, which replaced muscle, these technologies replace judgment, and the warning is that this time few new jobs will appear to absorb those displaced.

Text 2
Similar warnings have accompanied almost every new technology since the power loom, and yet total employment has generally grown over time as new kinds of work appeared. This history does not guarantee a smooth future, however. New jobs often require different skills and appear in different places, and the workers who lose old jobs are rarely the ones who fill the new ones.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the economists' warning in Text 1?
options: By arguing that history guarantees that every worker who loses a job will find a new one
By agreeing that automation will leave millions with no place in the economy
By doubting that work will vanish overall while granting that many may still suffer
By claiming that new technologies have always reduced the total number of jobs
explanation: Text 2 cites history to suggest total employment will grow, but warns that displaced workers rarely get the new jobs. It says history 'does not guarantee a smooth future', ruling out a guarantee for every worker.

stem:
Text 1
The Library of Alexandria is often said to have been destroyed in a single great fire, taking with it much of the learning of the ancient world. The story has made the library a symbol of how quickly knowledge can be lost. Paintings and films have often shown flames consuming its shelves of scrolls.

Text 2
Most historians now think the Library of Alexandria declined slowly over several centuries. Funding fell, scholars were expelled during political conflicts, and papyrus scrolls that were not regularly copied simply decayed. A fire in 48 BCE may have damaged part of the collection, but no single event destroyed it. Its end was quiet neglect rather than catastrophe.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
options: It argues that the Library of Alexandria never existed in the ancient world.
It explains why papyrus scrolls last longer than books printed on paper.
It confirms the account in Text 1 by giving the date of the single great fire.
It offers a more gradual account of the loss described in Text 1.
explanation: Text 1 describes sudden destruction by fire, while Text 2 describes slow decline over centuries and says 'no single event destroyed it'. The fire of 48 BCE is mentioned only as partial damage, not as confirmation.

stem:
Text 1
Organic farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, is often presented as the future of agriculture. Its supporters point out that organic farms tend to have healthier soils and more wildlife than conventional farms. Some argue that all farms should eventually switch to organic methods, which they see as kinder to both people and the land.

Text 2
On average, organic farms produce smaller harvests than conventional ones growing the same crops, though the gap varies widely between crops and regions. Feeding a growing population entirely through organic methods could therefore require more farmland, possibly at the expense of forests. Combining the best organic practices with careful use of fertilisers may be a more realistic path.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view in Text 1 that organic farming is the future of agriculture?
options: By noting that lower yields could make a complete switch costly to forests
By denying that organic farms have healthier soils or more wildlife than others
